title: The Exploitation of Symmetry Can Help Simplify Numerical Calculations
lead: A molecule's symmetry decides which operations leave it unchanged, as the build of a Rubik's cube decides its moves. Benzene's Hückel determinant, rewritten in a basis of symmetric combinations of its 2p orbitals, shows how much work that symmetry can save.
notes: Written by Delmar Larsen and Kristin LaRue and shared under the book's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; the Rubik's cube photograph, used with Wikipedia's permission, and the link to a video of the cube being solved are left out.
exercise_notes: The exercise is new and AI-written, its roots checked by computation; its Bloom level and concept tags were chosen by AI. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

exercises.source_id: However, any basis set can be used to represent the determinant
exercises.prompt:
Butadiene's Hückel determinant in the basis of its four carbon $2p_z$ orbitals is

$$ \left|\begin{array}{cccc}x&1&0&0\\1&x&1&0\\0&1&x&1\\0&0&1&x\end{array}\right|=0 $$

Rewrite it in the basis $\phi_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(p_1+p_4)$, $\phi_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(p_2+p_3)$, $\phi_3 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(p_1-p_4)$, $\phi_4 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(p_2-p_3)$, using the Hückel values ($x$ on the diagonal, 1 between bonded neighbours, 0 otherwise, orbitals orthonormal). The determinant falls into two $2 \times 2$ blocks.

  1. What is the positive root of the block made of $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$?
  2. What is the positive root of the block made of $\phi_3$ and $\phi_4$?

parts.hint: Every matrix element between a combination with a + sign and one with a − sign is zero.

answer.solution:
Each entry is $\langle\phi_i|\cdots|\phi_j\rangle$ expanded over the $p$ orbitals. For $\phi_1$ with itself, $\tfrac12(x + x) = x$, since $p_1$ and $p_4$ are not neighbours; for $\phi_1$ with $\phi_2$, $\tfrac12(1 + 0 + 0 + 1) = 1$; for $\phi_2$ with itself, $\tfrac12(x + x + 1 + 1) = x + 1$. In the same way $\phi_3$ with itself gives $x$, $\phi_3$ with $\phi_4$ gives $\tfrac12(1 - 0 - 0 + 1) = 1$ and $\phi_4$ with itself $\tfrac12(x + x - 1 - 1) = x - 1$. Every entry between $\phi_1$ or $\phi_2$ and $\phi_3$ or $\phi_4$ cancels to zero, so the determinant is block diagonal:

$$ \left|\begin{array}{cc}x&1\\1&x+1\end{array}\right| \left|\begin{array}{cc}x&1\\1&x-1\end{array}\right| = (x^2+x-1)(x^2-x-1) = 0 $$

a. $x^2 + x - 1 = 0$ gives $x = (-1 \pm \sqrt5)/2$, that is $0.618$ and $-1.618$. b. $x^2 - x - 1 = 0$ gives $x = (1 \pm \sqrt5)/2$, that is $1.618$ and $-0.618$. Together these are $\pm1.618$ and $\pm0.618$, the same four roots the original $4 \times 4$ determinant gives (Section 10.6).

footnotes.html: The orbitals are the carbons' $2p_z$ orbitals, perpendicular to the ring, as the basis $\{|2p_z\rangle\}$ below writes them; $2p_x$ is meant as $2p_z$.
The last entry is $H_{66} - ES_{66}$; the determinant prints $ES_{6}$.

assumes.text: A determinant in block-diagonal form is the product of the determinants of its blocks.

steps.cap: A $2 \times 2$ determinant is the product of its diagonal entries less the product of the other two.
